en: A line of stone warehouses along the shore of a small bay at the southernmost point of Cyprus, with a masonry breakwater now under water and quarries on the cliffs behind. John Leonard and Stella Demesticha surveyed it from 2000; Simon James of the University of Leicester, with Vicki Score as field director, has excavated since 2015. The digging killed the old idea of a lost port town: geophysics and trenching found no houses behind the warehouses, so the harbour was worked by people living in the villages across the middle of the peninsula and probably by Kourion. Lying inside a military base has left it one of the best preserved ancient ports in the Mediterranean.

Long stone buildings sharing a single alignment, several with internal partitions and walled yards, laid out in one short planned episode rather than growing piecemeal. Burnt deposits in some of them suggest workshops as well as stores.

en: A hundred-hectare stretch of coast about 10 km east of Larnaca and much the same distance from ancient Kition, surveyed intensively since 2003 by William Caraher, R. Scott Moore and David Pettegrew. The ground carries an Iron Age sanctuary, a Classical and Hellenistic fortification on the Vigla ridge, a Late Roman town beside a bay that has since silted solid, and a coastal battery of the Venetian or Ottoman period. Its interest is method as much as material: the project published its survey data openly through Open Context, and it puts on the map a substantial Cypriot coastal settlement that no ancient author names.

en: The most thoroughly published Late Roman village on Cyprus, dug in the Vasilikos valley by Marcus Rautman and Murray McClellan and published in 2003. Three basilicas of the sixth and early seventh centuries stood in a settlement of a few hundred people, along with houses, storerooms and pressing installations. Its pottery, tested by neutron activation, was mostly made from the valley's own clays, while the amphora kilns at Zygi-Petrini a few kilometres away were turning out the standard export jar of the eastern Mediterranean. Kopetra matters because it shows the Cypriot countryside was not a backwater but wired into the economy of the late empire.

Three churches for one modest village, all elaborately decorated, in the excavation areas the team called Kopetra, Sirmata and Spilios. Nobody has a wholly satisfying explanation for why a settlement this size needed three.

en: A small rural church a little inland from the south coast, in what was probably the territory of Amathus. A bulldozer went through it in 1991, and Sturt Manning's Maroni Valley survey recorded and salvaged what was left between 1990 and 1997. Two churches were found, one succeeding the other on the same spot: a nearly square building of the early to mid fifth century, replaced around 500 by a larger one with a polygonal apse. Modest as it is, it is one of the very few rural churches on the island to have been properly excavated and published.

An almost square church with large apses projecting from the east wall. The publication describes it as three-aisled, but its original arrangement seems to have been twin-aisled, which would be unusual in Early Christian architecture on Cyprus and has not been explained.

en: A rural site beside the chapel of Panayia Ematousa north of Aradippou, excavated by the University of Copenhagen between 1991 and 1999 as part of the teaching programme in classical archaeology and published in two volumes by the Danish Institute at Athens. Four periods of activity were found: Archaic to Early Classical, Hellenistic, Early Roman and Late Roman. Almost everything known about Hellenistic and Early Roman Cyprus comes from cities, so a farming settlement of those centuries dug and published in full is out of proportion to its size in importance.

Four distinct phases of use separated in the stratigraphy, running from the Archaic and Early Classical periods through the Hellenistic and Early Roman to a Late Roman occupation. The sequence, not any single object, is what the site is famous for.

en: Strabo names Ourania among the towns of the Karpas, and in 306 BCE the troops of Demetrius Poliorcetes landed at neighbouring Karpasia and took both towns before marching on Salamis. What a visitor sees now is later: three ruined churches in a row, a citadel cut into the living rock on the hill behind, rock-cut tombs, and the silted harbour below. Nothing at Aphendrika has been excavated to modern standards, which is why the dates given for its churches vary widely from one account to the next, and it sits in the occupied north with no prospect of work soon.
Byzantine, with a later chapel inserted
The largest of the three churches, a ruined basilica into which a smaller vaulted chapel was later built, a common Cypriot economy when a congregation shrank.
A domed church of ashlar masonry standing next to the Chrysiotissa, with its vaults partly intact.
The third and smallest of the group, which gave the whole site its modern name. The three standing side by side are the reason the place is visited at all.
A fortified outcrop behind the churches with chambers, stairs and cisterns cut into the rock itself, the most likely core of the ancient town.

en: Chamber tombs cut into the rock around the site, the necropolis of Ourania. They have been robbed repeatedly and never recorded properly.

A domed church of the eleventh or twelfth century built over a fifth-century basilica whose apse was deliberately kept, because of what it held: a mosaic of the Virgin between two archangels, one of the finest pieces of early Byzantine wall mosaic anywhere. The name means 'built by angels'. A small dig under the floor in 1959 found graves cut into the older foundations and traces of two earlier building phases, a columned basilica and then a pier basilica. Whether the old apse was reused to save labour or out of reverence for the mosaic is still argued.
The apse mosaic of the Virgin

The Virgin stands on a footstool with the Christ Child on her left arm, flanked by Michael and Gabriel whose wings are worked in peacock feathers, all against a gold ground. The angels hold a sceptre and offer a globe surmounted by a cross. Scholars compare the modelling of the faces to San Vitale at Ravenna and the type to the apse of Saint Catherine's in Sinai.

en: A church of many periods beside the Famagusta road, whose central apse belonged to a fifth-century basilica and whose vaults and dome were raised over the old plan, probably in the eleventh century. Its sixth-century apse mosaic was one of only a handful of Byzantine wall mosaics anywhere to survive Iconoclasm. The priests left in 1976; by November 1979 word reached the Department of Antiquities that the church had been stripped and was being used to stable animals, and that the mosaic had been cut out of the wall with axes. Recovering four of the fragments through the American courts produced the leading modern judgment on buying looted antiquities.
The apse mosaic of the Virgin enthroned

The Virgin sat on a throne with the Christ Child on her lap, two archangels attending, and the twelve apostles in medallions ringed with acanthus around the arch. The handling is looser and more impressionistic than the mosaic at Kiti; the date is still argued, but most put it in the sixth century alongside the work at Ravenna.

en: Autocephalous Church of Cyprus v. Goldberg

Judge Noland of the Southern District of Indiana awarded the mosaics to the Church of Cyprus in 1989, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed on 24 October 1990, holding that a buyer who asked so few questions in such suspicious circumstances could not take good title. The opinion's advice to dealers, to run a full background check on the seller and his claim, is now the standard citation for due diligence in the antiquities trade.

en: The shrine that made the Church of Cyprus independent. In about 477 Archbishop Anthemios announced that a vision had led him to the tomb of Barnabas, the apostle who was a Cypriot and who had preached on the island with Paul, with a copy of Matthew's gospel lying on his chest. The find let the archbishop appeal over the head of the patriarch of Antioch directly to the emperor. Zeno paid for a basilica on the spot and confirmed the Cypriot bishops' right to consecrate their own. The church standing today was built around 900 over the east end of the old one.

en: A single-aisled barrel-vaulted church five kilometres south of Nikitari, all that survives of the monastery of Phorbia founded in 1099 and abandoned in the eighteenth century. A dedicatory inscription dates the paintings to 1105/06 and names the donor, a court official, in the reign of Alexios I Komnenos. This is the earliest and the finest Komnenian fresco cycle on the island, and the church UNESCO put first when it listed the ten painted churches of the Troodos in 1985.

A panel on the south wall records that the church of the Holy Mother of God was painted at the urgent request and expense of a court official in the reign of the emperor Alexios Komnenos. The official's name is read as Nikephoros in most of the English literature and as Nikolaos in some Greek accounts, and the surname Ischyrios is not universally accepted.

en: A small church on the north-east slopes of Madari, named after the vetch that grows around it, holding the most complete late Komnenian painted programme in Cyprus. An inscription on the north lintel says the paintings were finished in December 1192 by a monk called Theodore Apseudis, trained in Constantinople, the same painter who had decorated the hermitage of Neophytos above Paphos nine years earlier. The patron names himself Leon, son of Authentes, a Byzantine aristocrat who had taken refuge nearby. It is the last great work of Byzantine Cyprus, finished a year after the island changed hands.
